A Norse camp at the northern tip of Newfoundland, the only confirmed site of Europeans in the Americas before Columbus. Wood there was cut with metal tools, and tree rings marked by a solar storm of 993 let scientists date the felling to exactly 1021.

The camp had eight turf buildings: halls, workshops and a smithy where bog iron was smelted. It housed perhaps a few dozen people for a short time, likely as a base for trips further south. Butternuts found on the site only grow further south. It fits the Icelandic sagas, which tell of Leif Erikson sailing to a land called Vinland.

The Norse came from the colonies in Greenland, founded about 985 by Erik the Red, an offshoot of Viking Age Scandinavia by way of Iceland. They did not stay. Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the site in 1960, proving the sagas held some truth. Lasting contact had to wait almost five centuries, until Columbus reached the Caribbean.
